findings.title: gold-runner --pack=value silently ran every case
findings.symptom: The equals form was not recognised; with no selector the runner ran all cases.
findings.evidence: PR #5 review

findings.title: Answers can be rewritten after review, so what was promised before the change is lost
findings.symptom: The gates read only the final answers file. In a second project running the same loop, about 70 existing answers were rewritten in place after review rounds (2026-10-17 to 10-21); the file still read as written before coding.

findings.direct_cause: No check compared the committed answers with the ones being committed.
why: Answering before the change was a rule in the docs, checked only as "the file has answers now".
Keeping answers true after a fix looked like hygiene, so rewriting them was the natural move.
findings.root_cause: A required step (answer before you build) was enforced only at one moment, not over time.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: answers files new on a branch are version 2; a committed answer and its guard never change; corrections are appended as revisions naming a finding; pre-commit compares with HEAD and CI walks every commit (R2)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-129: a committed answer cannot be rewritten at commit time
findings.sweep: Both enforcement points that read answers (pre-commit, CI range) now compare versions; the edit hook needs no comparison because it never accepts a commit.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-07 detectors check that gates pass exit codes through and that required steps run; none checks that an input the gate reads cannot be changed after the gate passed.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::an answer, once committed, is never rewritten: corrections are revisions naming a finding

findings.title: The answers check passes any 40 characters of prose, so a class recurs under the very question that was answered
findings.symptom: In the second project, all 91 findings logged since 2026-10-18 whose branch could be identified belong to a class whose question that branch had answered before coding; 73 of 80 upgraded no check. Nothing tied an answer to a check or recorded which answer failed.

findings.direct_cause: An answer was free text; the check could only fail for its form, never for whether it prevents anything.
why: The loop measured "was it answered", the only thing a text check can see.
A miss under an answered question was logged like any other finding, so the loop never learned which answers fail.
findings.root_cause: The check named "the history was considered" but could not fail when it was not applied.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a version-2 answer names its guard (a test that must resolve at commit and in CI, or "none: <reason>"); a finding introduced on a branch in a class that branch answered must carry answer_failed {qid, why}; the report counts them (R3, R4)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-130: an answer that names no guard is not an answer
findings.sweep: Applied at all three points that read answers; the report shows the miss rate. Ceiling stated: a guard that resolves can still be too weak (mutation work).
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-12 detectors check controls, refusal codes and timeouts of product checks; the loop's own answer rule was never asked to fail for its stated reason.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a finding added under an answered class names the answer that failed

findings.title: Stop-the-line is satisfied by a review document; the next change in a stopped class proceeds as before
findings.symptom: C-02, C-03, C-04, C-13 and C-15 each had two latest escapes with mechanism_upgrade "none", and the gate was green: a review file naming the findings released them.
findings.evidence: test/findings-ledger.test.mjs stop-line test (per root-cause axis, satisfied by text in findings/reviews/); findings-report 2026-10-21: detector upgrade rate 45% (34/76)
findings.direct_cause: The stop-line rule checked for a document, not for a check or a decision.
why: §15.4 was implemented as "write the review", the cheapest observable step.
Nothing refused work in the stopped class, so the review changed nothing downstream.
findings.root_cause: A required step (upgrade the check or stop) existed as a document requirement.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a stopped class refuses every change that must answer it — hook, pre-commit, CI — until findings/classes.json records a stopline for its latest escape: a detector the class lists and that resolves, a waiver, or debt not yet due (R5)

findings.title: The shell gate let git commands that rewrite working-tree files through as read-only
findings.symptom: Independent review of 7237bcb: git checkout -- <file>, git checkout <ref> -- <file>, git restore, git stash pop, git reset --hard and git clean were classified read, so a blocked agent could change or discard tracked files through them without answers; git config <key> <value> (e.g. core.hooksPath) also passed as a read.
findings.evidence: review repro in a harness repo: echo x > src/x.mjs exits 2, git checkout -- src/x.mjs exits 0; classifyShell put checkout, restore, stash, reset, clean in a hand list of "branch moves"
findings.direct_cause: A hand list (GIT_VCS) on the read-only side admitted subcommands that write files.
why: The rule "provably read-only" was applied to commands by name, and git was listed by subcommand name without asking what each does to the working tree.
The classifier table tested git reads and branch creation but no git subcommand that writes.
findings.root_cause: A list stood in for the rule on the side that lets things through.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: git is classified by what each command does to the working tree — pathspec checkouts, restore and rm/mv are writes with targets; stash push/pop/apply, reset --hard/--merge/--keep, clean, cherry-pick, revert, apply and config writes are opaque; only commands that create or move between existing commits pass

findings.sweep: Every git subcommand the classifier names was re-read for its effect on tracked files; npm install now names package.json and package-lock.json; npm ci, which writes only ignored files, passes.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02 detectors check docs, bundle keys and suite environments; the new classifier table was itself the detector and listed no git writes.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the shell classifier: every read-only form passes and every writing form is caught

findings.title: No guard was ever shown to fail before its fix

findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-139: a guard that already passes before the fix is refused

findings.title: The shell gate let git commands that turn the hooks off through, and offered no legitimate way to dispute a gate
findings.symptom: git commit --no-verify, git commit -n, git push --no-verify, git -c core.hooksPath=… and git config core.hooksPath passed the Claude Code shell gate once the answers existed (commit and push count as recording, not writing). A blocked agent had no sanctioned alternative to routing around the gate.
findings.evidence: anthropics/claude-code#40117 (Mar 2026): an agent used --no-verify across six commits despite memory and CLAUDE.md rules; ImpossibleBench (arXiv 2510.20270): giving agents an abort/flag option cut cheating from 54% to 9% for GPT-5; reproduced here on the evolve/close-bypasses checker
findings.direct_cause: The classifier judged git commit and push by whether they write files, not by whether they switch the hooks off.
why: Skipping hooks was treated as acceptable because CI re-checks the branch, but CI runs only on pull requests and work before a PR is unchecked.
Refusals said what to answer, never what to do when the gate itself is wrong.
findings.root_cause: A required step (run the hooks) could be skipped by a flag, and the only alternative to complying was to route around.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: the hook refuses --no-verify, commit -n and hooksPath changes outright; every refusal names `npm run inbox -- add --source dispute "<why>"`, which records the dispute and blocks commits until the owner resolves it
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-140: commands that turn the git hooks off are refused even with every answer given
findings.sweep: Push and merge forms of --no-verify are covered; the dispute path is added to the edit and shell refusals; CI and pre-commit already block an unresolved inbox item. Widened after the Codex/Cursor/Gemini research (2026-10-21): a shell wrapping a script (`bash -lc …`, the form Codex now sends — rsyslog 9d384cf), git configuration set through GIT_CONFIG_* variables, HUSKY=0 / SKIP=, merge and am -n, and plumbing that writes history without hooks (commit-tree, update-ref, replace, hash-object -w).
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-07 detectors check that gates run; none checks the flags that tell git not to run them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-140: commands that turn the git hooks off are refused even with every answer given

findings.title: A checker that cannot load locked out the edits that would repair it
findings.symptom: On 2026-10-22 the shell tokenizer was moved into src/classify.mjs before that file existed. findings-lib.mjs then failed to import, findings-check.mjs crashed before its own repair exemption could run, and the parent folder's dispatcher, which fails closed on a crash, denied every edit and every shell command in the repository for the rest of the session, including the edits that would have repaired it.
findings.evidence: hook refusals in the session transcript on Edit, Write and Bash: "ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND … src/classify.mjs … denied rather than let an unchecked call through"; work continued only as drafts outside the repository until the owner restored one file
findings.direct_cause: The repair exemption sat behind a static import that could fail.
why: The exemption was written for errors inside the check, not for the check failing to load.
The dispatcher was made fail closed without a repair path that does not depend on the component that fails.
findings.root_cause: The failure of one module took down the path meant to repair it.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: findings-check loads its library lazily; while it cannot load, edits to scripts/findings-*.mjs, src/classify.mjs and findings/ pass, and so does git restore of exactly those files; everything else is denied with the way to repair
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-141: while the checker cannot load, its code is restored from git, never rewritten
findings.class_fix: RC-09 stop-line review: the parent-folder dispatcher runs the gate from a copy taken from HEAD and kept outside the working tree, adopted only once it passes the self-test of the copy it replaces (scripts/gate-files.json lists the files, hooks and cases); the checker judges the repository the dispatcher names (SAKK_GATE_REPO), and while it cannot load only findings/ and restoring its committed code stay open.
findings.sweep: The parent dispatcher and the managed install keep failing closed; the repair path lives in the checker, the one component that knows its own files. Pre-commit and CI still fail while the checker cannot load. Narrowed after the RC-09 research: the catch-all after a check error no longer lets an edit of the gate code through either.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-09 detectors isolate failures on product paths and in scripts; none fed the loop's own checker a library that cannot load.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-141: while the checker cannot load, its code is restored from git, never rewritten

corrections.from: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-141: the gate's own files can be edited while the checker cannot load
corrections.why: The research behind the RC-09 review: a blanket exemption for the gate's own files lets a broken gate be rewritten unjudged, so the repair window is now restore-only and the guard test says so.

corrections.from: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-141: the gate's own files can be edited while the checker cannot load
corrections.why: The same test, renamed for what it now proves: the gate code is restored from git, never rewritten, while the checker cannot load.

findings.title: A review that could not run showed as a passed check
findings.symptom: pr-review.yml's adversarial-review job, with no DEEPSEEK_API_KEY in this repository, printed a notice and ended with exit 0, so every pull request carried a green check although no model review ran; the session's status report then counted it as passed. Three more paths in the same job did the same (a failed API call, an empty response, a review that could not be posted), and ci.yml's base-checker step exited 0 when the base had no checker.
findings.evidence: inbox 2026-10-22T07-21-52-808Z-2b4f48; the owner: the key was configured for the HostApp repository, not this one
findings.direct_cause: Skipping the work was written as a successful step.
why: The job could only say pass or fail, and skipped was spelled pass.
No check read the workflows for steps that end early with success.
findings.root_cause: A check that did not run reported success.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a review-key job says only whether a key is set; the review job runs only if it is (needs + if), so without a key it shows as skipped; once it runs, a failed call, an empty response or a review that cannot be posted fails the check; the base-checker step fails when the base has no checker
findings.guard: test/ci-honesty.test.mjs::no workflow turns a skip or a failure into a green check
findings.sweep: Every workflow in .github/workflows/ was read for exit 0, || true, || echo and continue-on-error: five uses, all in pr-review.yml and ci.yml, all fixed; the detector now runs on every workflow file.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-01 detectors read product commands and docs; none read the CI workflows that report on them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/ci-honesty.test.mjs::no workflow turns a skip or a failure into a green check

findings.title: A hung child held the test run for twenty minutes; --test-timeout cannot bound it
findings.symptom: During a local run of four test files in parallel, the checker spawned by test/self-evolution.test.mjs ('a command longer than the bound…') sat blocked reading its stdin while its parent waited in spawnSync; the test ran 1,223 s against a 300 s --test-timeout and the run had to be found and killed by hand. The hang itself did not recur in 392 tries (8×4 targeted parallel runs, 360 stress spawns with 70 KB stdin), so its direct cause is not known.
findings.evidence: session 2026-10-22: process 6803 sampled in read(0) under ReadFileUtf8; test output "a command longer than the bound is refused… (1223036 ms)"; scratchpad stdin-stress.mjs and repro.sh found no repeat
findings.direct_cause: Test helpers started synchronous children without a timeout.
why: A synchronous child blocks the event loop, so the timer behind --test-timeout cannot fire.
The C-04 detector checked that every node --test script carries --test-timeout and was read as bounding every test.
findings.root_cause: The test tool's own bound was trusted for a case it cannot see.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: test/bounded-spawn.mjs is loaded before every test file (--import in npm test, test:eval and the pre-commit hook) and gives every spawnSync, execFileSync and execSync without its own timeout a 240 s bound with SIGKILL, saying on stderr which child it killed
findings.guard: test/bounded-spawn.test.mjs::every node --test run loads the bound
findings.sweep: 115 synchronous spawns in test/ and eval/__tests__/ are now bounded by the preload rather than one by one; the detector covers npm scripts, scripts/hooks/ and .github/workflows/.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-04 detector proved every run carries --test-timeout, and --test-timeout cannot interrupt a synchronous child.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/bounded-spawn.test.mjs::every node --test run loads the bound

findings.title: The gate's files were listed by hand in five places, and one copy missed a file
findings.symptom: When the shell tokenizer moved to src/classify.mjs, the test of the base-branch checker still copied only scripts/findings-check.mjs and findings-lib.mjs, so the base checker failed to load ('Cannot find module …/src/classify.mjs') and the test failed for that reason instead of judging the branch. The same set was written out separately in both test harnesses, the CI base-checker step and the checker's repair path.
findings.evidence: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the base branch's checker judges the pull request too, 2026-10-22: "the checker cannot load (Cannot find module … src/classify.mjs …)"
findings.direct_cause: One test copied a fixed list of two files.
why: Each place that copies the gate wrote its own list.
Nothing compared those lists with what the checker imports.
findings.root_cause: A list written in each place stood in for the rule 'the files the gate runs from'.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: scripts/gate-files.json lists the files once; both harnesses, the base-checker test and the CI base-checker step read it (CI falls back to the old pattern only for a base from before the list)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the gate's files are listed once, and the list is what the checker loads (F-144)
findings.sweep: All five copies found by searching for findings-check.mjs and findings-lib.mjs across test/, scripts/ and .github/; the checker's repair path keeps its own pattern until the dispatcher's last-known-good snapshot (RC-09 review) replaces it, and the detector compares the list with the checker's real import closure.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02 detectors compare product rules with their lists; the gate's own file set was never one of them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the gate's files are listed once, and the list is what the checker loads (F-144)

findings.title: A wrapper's flag value was read as the command, so a force push behind sudo -u passed
findings.symptom: In the guard's classifier (M1 draft), `sudo -u root env FOO=1 command git push --force` skipped sudo's flags but not the value of -u, took `root` as the command's name and answered shell.run, which the shipped policy allows. The draft's own test caught it before any commit.
findings.evidence: test/guard.test.mjs::wrappers are unwrapped before the command is named, first run 2026-10-22: "sudo -u root env FOO=1 command git push --force" not destructive
findings.direct_cause: The unwrapper skipped words starting with - and nothing else.
why: Wrappers were a list of names; which of their flags take a value was not part of it.
The next literal word was taken as the command without the wrapper's grammar.
findings.root_cause: A list of wrapper names stood in for each wrapper's grammar.

answer_failed.why: C-02.1 said a call is a named action only when its form is recognised and anything else is shell.run; a wrapper form was recognised but misread, so the unknown-is-shell.run rule let a destructive command through as an ordinary one.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: WRAPPERS maps each wrapper to the flags that take a value and a sample; the value is skipped with its flag (sudo, doas, nice, time, timeout, exec; env -u/-S/-C)
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::every wrapper, with a flag that takes a value, still names the command it runs (F-145)
findings.sweep: Every wrapper in the list was given its value flags from its manual page; env handled the same way; the detector runs each wrapper's sample in front of a force push, and a wrapper added without a sample fails it.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02 detectors check lists against their rules in the ledger and policy code; the classifier's wrapper list is new in M1 and had none.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::every wrapper, with a flag that takes a value, still names the command it runs (F-145)

findings.title: A temp-folder allow covered the home folder, and deleting the repository itself had no name
findings.symptom: In the guard's shipped policy (M1 draft), allow-temp-cleanup matched ~outside/var/folders/ by prefix and came before deny-rm-outside-repo; with HOME inside a temp folder (the test world here, HOME=/tmp in many containers) `rm -rf ~/` and `rm -rf ~/work` were allowed. The same review showed that `rm -rf .` or `cd .. && rm -rf <repo>` gave the repository root no scope, so allow-in-repo answered allow.
findings.evidence: test/guard.test.mjs::the shipped policy denies the headline cases and ::deletes outside the repository are denied through every alias, first runs 2026-10-22: "rm -rf ~/" allow
findings.direct_cause: Folder allows were judged on the target path alone.
why: The home folder had no name of its own, only whatever absolute path it sits at.
A delete was named for its target, not for what lies under it: the repository, home, Sakk state.
findings.root_cause: One folder had several names, and the one a rule saw depended on where it happened to live.

answer_failed.why: C-08.1 gave every path one canonical name, but the home folder's name was its absolute path, so a temp-folder prefix could cover it, and a delete of a parent was named for the parent instead of for the repository or home inside it.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: paths under the home folder are ~home/…; a delete whose target contains the repository, the home folder or SAKK_HOME is ~protected/repo|home|sakk; the shipped policy denies ~protected/ first and ~home/ with ~outside/
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::a delete that takes the repository, the home folder or Sakk state with it is denied before any allow (F-146)
findings.sweep: Every allow in the shipped policy was read for a folder prefix: allow-temp-cleanup was the only one; mv of the repository, find -delete on a parent and rm of ~/.sakk now name what they take; spec and docs list the new scopes.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-08 detectors check that aliases of one path reach one name; none checked what a folder rule covers when the folder contains another protected one.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::a delete that takes the repository, the home folder or Sakk state with it is denied before any allow (F-146)

findings.title: The drill check assumed one-letter ids and missed the 27th drill
findings.symptom: test/core-specs.test.mjs looked for each core file's drill with /run_drill MUT-[A-Z] file /, written in 458c86d when there were fewer than 26 drills; the guard's drills MUT-AA…AE were not recognised and the three new core files read as undrilled.
findings.evidence: test/core-specs.test.mjs, 2026-10-22: "src/hook.mjs: has a spec and a mutation-drill anchor — no drill anchor"
findings.direct_cause: The id pattern matched one letter.
why: The format of an id was never stated, only assumed from the ids that existed.
No test ran the pattern against an id past Z.
findings.root_cause: A state that was true while the registry was small was taken as a rule.

answer_failed.why: C-09.1 listed the environments the hook is tried in (no repository, detached HEAD, Node 20 and 22) and not the state of the registries this branch adds to; the 27th drill was a state no check had tried.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: one drillLine() pattern takes ids of any length, used by every core-file test
findings.guard: test/core-specs.test.mjs::every drill entry is recognised, however many letters its id has (F-147)
findings.sweep: Other id patterns read for the same assumption: findings (F-\d+), questions (C-\d+\.\d+) and classes take any number of digits; drill ids were the only fixed-width one.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-09 detectors try environments; none tried a registry grown past the size it was written at.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/core-specs.test.mjs::every drill entry is recognised, however many letters its id has (F-147)

findings.title: The guard spec's rule table differed from the shipped policy
findings.symptom: specs/guard/spec.md listed the shipped rules without allow-temp-cleanup, in an order other than the policy's, with two rules folded into one row; rules match first to last, so the table described a policy that does not exist.
findings.evidence: review of specs/guard/spec.md against policies/guard-default.json while fixing F-146, 2026-10-22
findings.direct_cause: The table was written by hand beside the policy.
why: Nothing compared the table with the policy file.
The order of rules, which decides the answer, was not part of what the table had to match.
findings.root_cause: A statement about the policy was kept by memory.

answer_failed.why: C-05.1 made the docs and the spec's adversary rows name tested behaviour, but the spec's rule table was outside both, so it drifted from the policy file with nothing to fail.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the table lists every shipped rule, one per row, in the policy's order, with its verdict
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::the spec lists the shipped rules in their order, with their answers (F-148)
findings.sweep: docs/GUARD.md names no rule list of its own (it points to the policy file); the README quick start names behaviour only.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-05 detectors check that named codes and tests exist; none compared a spec table with the file it describes.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::the spec lists the shipped rules in their order, with their answers (F-148)

findings.title: Drill anchors drifted from the source four times, and only the hour-long drill noticed
findings.symptom: While building M1, prettier's line wrapping broke new drill anchors (MUT-AB, MUT-AC) and two later edits broke MUT-AA (the halt line was rewritten) and MUT-AD (the anchor came to appear twice in src/classify.mjs). Each was found only when the mutation drill ran, about an hour per full run; the plan's step 're-check every drill anchor after prettier' was done by hand and missed two.
findings.evidence: scratchpad drill-m1.out, 2026-10-22: "[MUT-AA] DRILL BROKEN: anchor not found exactly once in src/hook.mjs", "[MUT-AD] … src/classify.mjs"
findings.direct_cause: Anchors are literal source text, and only the drill read them.
why: The drill is slow, so it runs before merge, not on each change.
Re-checking anchors after an edit was a step in a plan, done from memory.
findings.root_cause: A required check was kept as a written step instead of a test.

answer_failed.why: C-10.1 moved the guard's required steps into the hook itself, but this branch's own step of re-checking drill anchors after an edit or a reformat stayed a line in a plan, so two anchors drifted unseen until the drill ran.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: MUT-AA and MUT-AD point at the current source; npm test reads every drill anchor the way run_drill receives it (double- or single-quoted) and fails when one is not found exactly once
findings.guard: test/core-specs.test.mjs::every drill anchor is found exactly once in its file, without running the drill (F-149)
findings.sweep: All 32 drill entries are read by the new test; it also fails if an entry is laid out so that it cannot be read, so none is skipped.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-10 detectors turn rule text into checks for the product; the drill's anchors were checked only by the drill itself.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/core-specs.test.mjs::every drill anchor is found exactly once in its file, without running the drill (F-149)

findings.title: The F-105 input bounds locked settled money and missed non-string inputs
findings.symptom: A reservation made before ids were bounded (the old MCP allowed 4096-char callIds) could never be settled: settle refused the long callId with INPUT_TOO_LONG, so its estimate held the cap for ever, and a failedUnknownCost one jammed the ledger with no way out but hand-editing. Separately, a non-string runId (array) or taskId (object), and the tokens and reconciliation reason, skipped the string-only length check and were stored whole, so the growth F-105 is about was still open to direct library callers.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22, scripts in scratchpad/rev (r1.mjs, r2.mjs)
findings.direct_cause: checkLength only bounded strings and ran on a looked-up id, not just stored ones.
why: The bound was written for ids as they are stored, and settle/resume also pass an id that is only looked up.
checkLength skipped any value that was not a string, so a non-string was neither bounded nor refused.
Old ledgers with long ids were never replayed against the new bound.
findings.root_cause: A bound for newly stored input was assumed to be safe on every id, including ones only looked up and ones not yet proven to be strings.

answer_failed.why: C-04.1 bounded the hook's payload and command; it did not cover the ledger's own stored fields, so a length check added for them was applied too broadly (a looked-up id) and too narrowly (strings only).

findings.instance_fix: this commit: settle and resume no longer length-bound a looked-up id (a long reservation still settles); checkLength refuses a non-string stored field (INPUT_INVALID) as well as an over-long one; tokens is bounded (object, <=4096 bytes); reconciliation reasons are truncated, never refused, so a long id cannot jam the books.
findings.guard: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::a non-string runId, taskId or tokens is refused, not stored whole (F-150)
findings.sweep: Every stored field of the ledger was checked: ids and names bounded or refused by type; tokens bounded; reasons truncated; looked-up ids (settle callId, resume agentId) left unbounded on purpose so old entries still resolve.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-04 detector listed reserve with one over-long-string case; it never fed a non-string field or an old long id.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::a non-string runId, taskId or tokens is refused, not stored whole (F-150)

distinct_from.F-105: F-105 is the books growing O(n) with use (the archive fixes that, still open); F-150 is that the input bounds added for F-105 first part were applied wrongly — to a looked-up id and to strings only — a correctness bug in those bounds, not the growth itself.

findings.title: The C-04 cost-bounds detector had guards that could never fail
findings.symptom: Three BOUNDS entries (markReconciliationRequired, totalsOf, defaultLedgerPath) named a guard that was a test inside cost-bounds.test.mjs itself, and resolves() only checked the name was a substring of the file, so deleting the real bound left the suite green. No test covered runId or taskId at all.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22: deleting the runId/taskId checks kept ledger-bounds and cost-bounds green
findings.direct_cause: resolves() matched any substring, and a guard could point at the listing that requires it.
why: A guard was allowed to name the meta-test that only checks the function is listed.
A substring match accepted a comment or the entry text itself as if it were a test.
findings.root_cause: The detector checked that a guard was named, not that it was a real test that fails when the bound is gone.

answer_failed.why: C-03.1 asks whether a check fails for the reason it names; the cost-bounds detector itself had guards that pass whatever the code does, so the question was answered for the product checks but not for this detector.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: resolves() accepts only a real test('<name>') declaration and refuses the circular meta-test; the three circular entries now point at real tests (a truncation test, an env test) or are marked F-105 debt; new tests cover non-string runId/taskId/tokens.
findings.guard: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::a huge reconciliation reason is stored truncated, not whole
findings.sweep: Every bounded entry re-checked: each now names a real falsifiable test or an open-finding debt; the meta-test can no longer be used as a guard.
findings.mechanism_gap: A self-check (the detector that proves functions are bounded) was not itself checked for the C-03 shape.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::a huge reconciliation reason is stored truncated, not whole

findings.title: status reported a max reservable amount the estimate floor refuses
findings.symptom: sakk status and the MCP totals reported max_reservable_usd = cap - committed - 1e-6, which could be a positive amount below the new estimate floor (1e-6); reserving exactly that figure returned ESTIMATE_INVALID, so the number the tool promised did not work when acted on.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22 (r3.mjs): cap 1, committed 0.9999985, reported ~5e-7, reserve refused
findings.direct_cause: The figure subtracted a hair for the cap but ignored the estimate floor.
why: The floor was added to reserve but the status figure was not revisited.
The figure was computed in two places by hand, so neither matched reserve exactly.
findings.root_cause: A reported figure was not derived from the same rule that acts on it.

answer_failed.why: C-05.2 asks whether every figure the tool reports works when acted on; the floor made a small positive max_reservable unreservable, and the figure was not rechecked against reserve.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: maxReservableUsd() in the ledger is the single source, used by status and MCP; it returns 0 whenever the headroom is below the floor, and otherwise an amount reserve() accepts.
findings.guard: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::max reservable is 0 when the headroom is below the floor
findings.sweep: The figure is computed once in the ledger and reused; both call sites (bin/sakk.mjs, src/mcp.mjs) import it instead of recomputing.
findings.mechanism_gap: No test reserved the exact amount status reported.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/cost-bounds.test.mjs::max reservable is 0 when the headroom is below the floor

distinct_from.F-104: F-104 is the lock/crash/fsync durability promises in the ledger; F-152 is a reported status figure (max_reservable) that did not match what reserve accepts — a reporting bug, unrelated to locking.

findings.title: The classifier waved through any command it did not model
findings.symptom: A command not in the classifier's recognised set fell to shell.run and was allowed whatever it touched. dd overwrote files (including the guard's own policy and .github/workflows/), rsync --delete and tar --remove-files destroyed files outside the repository, and perl/ruby in-place edits wrote files — none were classified as writing or deleting.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard guard surface, 2026-10-22 (findings 1 and 3)
findings.direct_cause: The write and delete handling was a fixed list of command names; the default for the rest was shell.run.
why: The classifier enumerated the commands it knew rather than deriving write/delete from the arguments.
An unmodelled command was assumed to touch nothing.
findings.root_cause: A list of recognised commands stood in for the rule "what writes or deletes files".

answer_failed.why: C-02.1 said an unrecognised form becomes shell.run and reaches the policy's later rules; but shell.run names no path, so the destructive-write and destructive-delete rules had nothing to match, and the call was allowed.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: dd (if=/of=), tar (archive/members/extract/--remove-files), rsync (--delete, --remove-source-files) and perl/ruby -i are modelled as the writes and deletes they perform.
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::commands that move or destroy files are modelled, not waved through (F-153)
findings.class_fix: A command the classifier does not model, whose arguments name a path, is no longer assumed to touch nothing: a secret file in them is a secret.read (F-155), and the modelled movers/destroyers above name their writes and deletes.
findings.sweep: The reviewer-named writers/destroyers (dd, tar, rsync, perl/ruby -i) are modelled; overwrite-to-destroy outside the repo is now a file.write that ask-write-outside catches.
findings.mechanism_gap: The classifier table test checked known destructive forms and ordinary work; it never fed a destructive command outside the known set.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::commands that move or destroy files are modelled, not waved through (F-153)

findings.title: find -exec and xargs running a remover were waved through
findings.symptom: find with -exec/-execdir/-ok ran a command on each match but was classified shell.run, so `find <path> -exec rm {} +` deleted outside the repository while `find -delete` was correctly caught. xargs feeding a remover was shell.run too.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22 (finding 4)
findings.direct_cause: find -exec and xargs were not inspected for the command they run.
why: Only find -delete was modelled; -exec was left as shell.run.
xargs' command is built from stdin and was treated as ordinary work.
findings.root_cause: The delete path through a runner (find -exec, xargs) was not enumerated, so it was assumed harmless.

answer_failed.why: C-02.2 asks where else the same rule applies; -delete was modelled but the equivalent -exec rm and xargs rm were not, so the rule 'a delete is a delete' was fixed in one place only.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: find -exec/-ok inspects the inner command (a remover deletes the roots, a reader reads them, anything else writes them); xargs feeding anything but a reader is shell.constructed (built at run time).
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::find -exec and xargs running a remover are modelled (F-154)
findings.sweep: Both runners (find -exec/-execdir/-ok/-okdir and xargs) are covered; the inner command is classified, not the runner name.
findings.mechanism_gap: find was tested only with -delete.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::find -exec and xargs running a remover are modelled (F-154)

findings.title: A secret read by a command not in the reader list was allowed
findings.symptom: secret.read is the guard's first line, but reading a secret file through a command outside the reader list (base64, openssl, dd if=) was shell.run and allowed.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22 (finding 5)
findings.direct_cause: Secret reads were recognised only for a fixed set of reader commands.
why: The reader list enumerated cat/head/grep and friends; anything else reading a secret was not seen.
The classifier never checked a command's path arguments against the secret-file pattern once the command was unrecognised.
findings.root_cause: A list of reader commands stood in for the rule "reading a secret file".

answer_failed.why: C-02.1 routed unknown commands to shell.run; a shell.run that happens to read a secret file by name was then allowed, because the secret-read rule only fired for named readers.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: any unmodelled command whose argument names a secret file is a secret.read, so the first line holds whatever command does the reading.
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::a secret read by a command not in the reader list is still a secret read (F-155)
findings.sweep: The secret-file catch runs for every command that reaches the fallthrough, not a fixed reader list.

findings.title: A git value-option read its value as the subcommand, hiding a force push
findings.symptom: git's own options that take a separate-word value (for example --namespace x) were not all registered, so the value word was read as the subcommand and the real push --force / reset --hard / branch -D was never classified — allowed as shell.run.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of oss/m1-guard, 2026-10-22 (finding 2)
findings.direct_cause: The git global-option skip listed only -C, -c, --git-dir, --work-tree as value-taking.
why: Which git options take a value was a short list, not the full set.
The token after the options was taken as the subcommand without checking it is one.
findings.root_cause: A list of value-taking options stood in for git's option grammar — the same shape as the wrapper flags in F-145.

answer_failed.why: C-02.1 relies on recognising a call's form; a recognised git form was misparsed because an unlisted value-option shifted the subcommand, so a destructive git command was read as ordinary and allowed.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: more value-taking git options are registered, and if the word after the options is not a judged subcommand the scan continues to the first one that is, so a value cannot stand in for the subcommand.
findings.guard: test/guard.test.mjs::a git value-option before a destructive subcommand does not hide it (F-156)
findings.sweep: git option parsing joins the wrapper-flag fix (F-145): both skip value words, and git additionally falls back to finding a real subcommand.
findings.mechanism_gap: The wrapper-flag fix (F-145) covered sudo/env/nice; git's own options were not revisited.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/guard.test.mjs::a git value-option before a destructive subcommand does not hide it (F-156)

findings.title: The broken-checker window and the loop classifier trusted inputs they should have resolved or refused
findings.symptom: The gate review found four holes the gate trusted rather than resolved: (1) while the checker could not load, the window judged a path by its leaf name, so a symlink leaf under findings/ pointing at product code passed; (2) it read a file_path key even on a Bash call, so a stray key made a shell write look like a file edit; (3) a checker library that threw a non-error (throw null/'x'/{}) crashed the window with exit 1 instead of denying, and code that read exit 1 as success would proceed; (4) the loop's shell classifier treated `node --test` as read-only regardless of code-injecting flags, so `node --test --import <payload>` ran arbitrary code unjudged.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of the gate and CI, 2026-10-22 (findings 4, 5, 6, and the node --test note); scripts in scratchpad/rev
findings.direct_cause: Each input was taken at face value: a path by its leaf, a payload by a key, a thrown value as an Error, a node flag list as harmless.
why: The window realpath-resolved only the parent directories, not the leaf.
The thrown value was assumed to be an Error with a .message.
node was assumed read-only whenever its first argument was --test, without reading the injecting flags.
findings.root_cause: The gate trusted the shape of its inputs instead of resolving or validating them.

answer_failed.why: C-07.1 said the payload, command and paths are canonicalized and bounded; but the window resolved only a path's parents (not its leaf), trusted a file_path key regardless of tool, and trusted a thrown value as an Error, and the loop classifier trusted node --test without its injecting flags.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the window realpaths the full path including the leaf; it treats a file_path only for a real file tool, judging a Bash call by its command; a non-error load failure is coerced to a printable message and still denies; node --test is read-only only when it injects no module (no --import/--require/-r/--loader/-e/--eval).
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-157: the window resolves a symlink leaf, survives a non-error, and ignores a stray key
findings.sweep: The window and the loop classifier were walked for inputs trusted by shape: path leaves, payload keys, thrown values, interpreter flags; each now resolves or validates. The review also showed the batch's own detectors trusted narrow inputs: the bounded-spawn preload missed an explicit null/undefined options slot and the scripts that spawn node --test with an argv array, and the ci-honesty detector missed many skip-to-green shapes and was fooled by an "exit 1" inside a message. Both are strengthened, and the unbounded script spawns (findings-proof, audit, attack-asr) now carry a timeout.
findings.mechanism_gap: The F-141 window tests exercised plain paths and a missing module; none used a symlink leaf, a stray key, a non-error throw, or an injecting node flag.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-157: the window resolves a symlink leaf, survives a non-error, and ignores a stray key

findings.title: The CI base checker ran after the PR’s own checker in the same workspace
findings.symptom: The self-evolution CI job ran the PR's own scripts/findings-check.mjs first and the base's checker second, in one workspace. The PR controls the first script, so it could move HEAD to the base (an empty range) or write $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_PATH before the base checker ran, defeating the check whose whole point is that a pull request cannot loosen the gate that judges it.
findings.evidence: adversarial review of the gate and CI, 2026-10-22 (finding 2): a PR whose checker ran `git checkout --detach <base>; exit 0` left the base-checker step an empty range that passed
findings.direct_cause: The untamperable check shared a workspace with, and ran after, PR-controlled code.
why: Both checks were steps of one job, so they shared a checkout and environment files.
The base checker computed its range from the ambient HEAD, which an earlier step could move.
findings.root_cause: A check meant to be beyond the pull request’s reach was not isolated from the pull request’s own code.

answer_failed.why: C-10.2 asks whether a step can be skipped by another route; the base checker could be neutralised by the PR's own earlier step in the same job — a route the answer did not consider.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the base checker is its own CI job with a fresh checkout and runner, so no PR code has run in it and its HEAD and environment are untampered; the PR’s own checker job can no longer reach it.
findings.guard: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the base branch's checker judges the pull request too
findings.sweep: The self-evolution job is asserted not to contain the base checker, and the base-checker job is asserted to be a pull_request job that reads the base scripts with git show.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-09 isolation work covered the gate at edit and dispatch time; it did not look at the CI job graph, where a required check shared a workspace with PR code.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the base branch's checker judges the pull request too

distinct_from.F-116: F-116 is that a red CI does not block a merge until main has branch protection (a GitHub setting); F-158 is that one CI check could be made to pass falsely by the PR's own earlier step — a workspace-isolation bug in the job graph, not branch protection.

findings.title: sakk ledger verify claimed an intact history but never checked the index, and false-failed on float drift
findings.symptom: The adversarial review of the F-105 archive found the cold trail's audit was not what it claimed: (1) HIGH — the call-id index is the only cross-history duplicate guard, but sakk ledger verify walked only the segment chain, so a lost index shard silently re-admitted a sealed call-id (a double-spend) and verify still reported SOUND; (2) the segment chain is an unkeyed sha256 with its tip in the writable hot file, so verify's 'intact and unaltered' wording over-claimed — it detects accidental corruption and loss, not a writer who recomputes the hashes; (3) LOW — verify folded the settled total per entry while maybeSeal accumulated it per segment, so float non-associativity could make an intact chain fail its own audit; (4) LOW — sakk ledger export --out failed with a raw Node stack instead of a typed code.
findings.evidence: independent adversarial review of oss/f105-archive, 2026-10-22 (HIGH index loss, MEDIUM unauthenticated chain, two LOW); reproductions r1-index-loss, r2-float-drift, r3-tamper, r4-export-out
findings.direct_cause: verify checked the chain but not the index, and recomputed the total in a different order than it was stored.
why: The index was treated as a derived cache, so the audit that vouches for the history did not include it.
The recompute and the maintained summary used different float-summation orders with a fixed absolute tolerance.
The audit's wording promised tamper-evidence the unkeyed, hot-anchored chain cannot give.
findings.root_cause: An audit named a guarantee (intact, unaltered, no reused call-id) stronger than what it actually checked.

answer_failed.why: C-03.1 asks whether a check fails for the reason it names and only that; verify named integrity of the whole history but did not check the index (missed a double-spend), over-claimed tamper-evidence, and could false-fail on an intact chain from float order.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: verify also rebuilds the expected index from cold and fails if any sealed call-id is missing or wrong; reserve refuses when segments are sealed but the whole index is gone; sakk ledger reindex rebuilds it; verify sums the total per segment exactly as maybeSeal does (no float false-fail); the spec states verify detects accidental corruption and loss, not tampering by a writer who can recompute the unkeyed hashes; export --out wraps its write error as a typed LEDGER_EXPORT_FAILED.
findings.guard: test/ledger-archive.test.mjs::verify catches a lost index, and reserve refuses rather than re-admit a sealed call-id
findings.sweep: verify now covers both the chain and the index; the reserve-time wholesale-loss guard and reindex give a fail-closed path and a recovery; the float summation matches in both places; the spec and CLI no longer claim tamper-evidence the design does not provide (out-of-band signing is a named later milestone).
findings.mechanism_gap: The archive tests checked the chain (flipped byte, broken link, wrong tip) but never a lost index, and the integrity claim was not read back against what verify actually walked.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/ledger-archive.test.mjs::verify catches a lost index, and reserve refuses rather than re-admit a sealed call-id

distinct_from.F-113: F-113 is the policy fuzz deciding pass/fail by a clock; F-159 is the ledger archive audit under-checking (no index check, wrong integrity claim, float false-fail) — a different check in a different module.

findings.title: A spend test passed only on 2026-10-22: its logs were dated that day while the hook read the real clock
findings.symptom: From 2026-10-23 the commit gate on oss/gitleaks-port failed test/spend.test.mjs 'the cap denies inside the hook's evaluate' ('allow' !== 'deny'). The same test fails on the unmodified branch head, and every branch from oss/m2-spend up carries it, so each CI re-run from that day on goes red.
findings.evidence: Local gate on 2026-10-23 (Asia/Dubai, 09:44Z): the one failure in the full run; reproduced alone with node --test --test-name-pattern='cap denies inside' on a clean checkout of 57e5958.
findings.direct_cause: The test wrote a session log stamped 2026-10-22T10:00Z and called evaluate() without its now option, so the hook took Date.now() as 'today' and the logged spend fell on yesterday.
why: Every capCheck test in the file passed now: NOW, but the two that go through evaluate() did not; evaluate defaults now to Date.now.
The test was written and first run on 2026-10-22, the only day its fixtures and the real clock agree, so it passed every local and CI run that day.
Nothing checks that a test with dated fixtures also fixes the clock the code under test reads.
findings.root_cause: A test assumed the day it runs equals the day its fixtures are stamped; the code took its clock from the environment, and that other environment (any later day) was never tried.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: both evaluate() calls in test/spend.test.mjs pass now: () => NOW, the log's mtime is set to NOW, and the test also asserts the same logs allow on the next day — the hook's clock, not the run date, decides 'today'. Product code was right: evaluate passes now() to the cap check.
findings.guard: test/spend.test.mjs::the cap denies inside the hook's evaluate, not only in capCheck
findings.sweep: Every evaluate() and capCheck() call in test/spend.test.mjs is read by the new detector (all now carry now). The other suites that call evaluate() configure no cap, so the run date does not reach a decision; the full gate on 2026-10-23 had this as its only failure.
findings.mechanism_gap: No check tied dated fixtures to a fixed clock; the suite was green on the day it was written and so could not show the dependency.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend.test.mjs::every hook or cap call in the spend tests sets its own clock (F-165)

distinct_from.F-62: F-62 is a stopwatch deciding pass/fail under load (C-04, a duration); F-165 is a calendar date assumed equal to the run date (C-09), which fails deterministically from the next day.
